comments.author: @JacquelynRivera930
comments.text: I live in the Bucks County suburbs the surround Philly in a neighborhood that couldn't be anymore opposite than the city. I'm about a 30 minute drive to Kensington, Philadelphia in Yardley, PA. My heroin addiction started out from an opioid addiction due to two bad car accidents I was in. I went through two years of physical therapy, while prescribed Percocet, OxyContin and Morphine. The day my physical therapy ended, so did my prescription medications. This was back in 2008/2009, and the medical field had yet to understand "addiction". I suffered immensely over the week I didn't have my medication, so I found it being sold in my neighborhood by teens and young adults like me. A few years later the opioid crisis and addiction from OxyContin 40 MG and 80 MG tablets were starting to come to light. The drug manufacturers of OxyContin changed the chemical makeup of the pill so people couldn't abuse it by crushing it and snorting it, injecting it or smoking it. I only snorted it, and I didn't know anyone who did anything other than snort it, so when that happened, we all turned to Percocet 30 MG pills that we could still crush and snort. They eventually became way too expensive at $25-$30 a piece needing 3-4+ a day, and after a few years of saying I'd never in a million years do heroin, I tried it! I snorted it for a while until one of my childhood best friends finally persuaded me to shoot it. I'd pay her in bags to shoot me up, and this was great for her because she was starting to not be able to afford her habit. She started stealing, eventually moved to Philly, sold the heroin, stole from store and pawned things, and she was arrested and sentenced to two years in the state penitentiary. I was a little luckier. I had always had a job, and I started working for a family friend's construction company doing the office work. One day I had overheard the boss talking about how he needed laborers, so I asked if I could get a few hours doing labor, and at first he laughed, but then he agreed! I ended up becoming a carpenter and starting my own business a few years later. It's interesting because throughout all of this, I remained on drugs, but no one had any idea because I had a house, cars, a thriving business, I did good work, I'm extremely intelligent, and I kept up with my appearance. Fast forward to Covid, and the heroin changed to fentanyl, and shortly after, fentanyl changed to xylazine. I had an almost 2 decade heroin/fentanyl/tranq addiction with multiple failed attempts to get sober. I honestly thought I'd never be free of it. I remember looking at people I walked past in the grocery store or at the mall and wondering how they were able to live a life without drugs? It got to a point where I envied them. It was horrible to see all of "street zombies" in Philly when I picked up my stash for the month. They'd be folded in half standing in the road, stuck between a door and the door frame of a corner store bent over trying to enter it, and you'd see people really high or withdrawing horribly. It got to a point where I could no longer find veins because the xylazine blew out most of them, and if I missed, it'd become a laceration that started from the inside of my flesh out. I seriously couldn't take it anymore, so I went back to snorting it, hated the taste, stopped using as much because of it, and so finally just stopped using all together. Today I'm sober, and I thank god it was before I truly ruined my body and physical appearance, my business, my bank account, my relationships, lifestyle, etc.. I wouldn't wish that addiction on my worst enemy, so I do have empathy for some of these people, but not all of them. Most of those Philadelphia drug addicts are complete scumbags. They shoot up on the street right in front of children walking to and from school, or throw their used disease filled needles where people and children play or walk to and from school, the bus or the train. I have ZERO empathy for a dirty waste of life that doesn't give a damn about the children and people who don't have an addiction that have to see and live with those filthy addicts. They have a choice, and they can put their needles in a trash can and/or bag, or bring them to a needle exchange instead of throwing them onto the streets where people, children and pets play and walk. It's just absolutely disgusting, and those people need to be thrown into jail and charged with attempted murder if any of their discard used needles infect another person. During my almost 20 year addiction never did I ever use and then drive a vehicle. I'd wait until I was home for the night to do my drugs, and so NEVER did it in front of people or children.
